Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which relies on the overlap of many opaque Gaussians to form shapes, BG-Triangle maintains distinct, sharp boundaries between primitives, making it particularly suitable for vectorization and compact scene representation [S1].

The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states that BG-Triangle uses Bézier triangles for geometry (which have sharp boundaries) and 3D Gaussian sub-primitives for appearance. It notes that 'unlike in 3DGS, the Gaussians in our setting are generated on the fly... but not opacity, since the geometry is defined by the Bézier triangles.' It further explains that the pipeline maintains 'sharp boundaries' by treating boundary points as isotropic Gaussians to soften the influence only at the discontinuities, while the core geometry remains distinct. This supports the claim that it maintains distinct, sharp boundaries between primitives (defined by the Bézier surfaces) unlike standard 3DGS which relies on overlapping opaque Gaussians.

The rasterization and splatting are similar in complexity to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, but with additional overhead for boundary detection and attribute interpolation from Bézier control points [S1].

The claim states that the complexity is 'similar to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting'. However, the provided evidence describes a significantly more complex pipeline involving tessellation of Bézier triangles into flat triangles, traditional rasterization to generate coordinate and index maps, boundary detection (marking pixels with different primitive IDs), and on-the-fly generation of Gaussian sub-primitives with specific attribute interpolation methods (barycentric for color, multi-resolution maps for other attributes). Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting does not involve Bézier geometry, tessellation, or this specific boundary-aware splatting mechanism. Therefore, the evidence suggests the complexity is different (likely higher due to the additional steps), not similar, and does not support the claim of similarity.
